articles.title: Migrating an Application to the Cloud: Node.js Graceful Shutdown
articles.excerpt: When you're migrating an application to the cloud and every deploy causes a short burst of 502s, the fix is usually two small changes. Give your Node.js service honest health check endpoints, and make…
articles.body: When you're migrating an application to the cloud and every deploy causes a short burst of 502s, the fix is usually two small changes. Give your Node.js service honest health check endpoints, and make it shut down gracefully when it gets SIGTERM. Together they make the load balancer stop sending traffic to an instance before that instance stops answering. Maybe you just containerised a service that ran fine on one VM for years, and now your error graph jumps for half a minute every time you ship. If so, this is almost certainly the cause. Your business logic is fine. The service has simply never had to shut down cleanly before. Why do rolling deploys drop requests? A rolling deploy starts new instances and then stops the old ones. The trouble is timing.

articles.title: How to reword README and docs text so developers actually get it
articles.excerpt: Most docs aren't wrong. They're written by the person who knows the code best, at the moment they know it best. That's the problem. Every shortcut makes sense to the author and almost none of it makes…
articles.body: Most docs aren't wrong. They're written by the person who knows the code best, at the moment they know it best. That's the problem. Every shortcut makes sense to the author and almost none of it makes sense to someone cloning the repo for the first time. You don't need to rewrite your docs from scratch. You need to reword the parts people read first and the parts they hit when something breaks. Here's how to do that for README intros, API descriptions, error messages and jargon. Rule zero. Protect the literal strings Before you change a single word, mark everything that has to stay exact. That means function names, flags, environment variables, file paths, config keys, version numbers and status codes. Wrap them in backticks if they aren't already.

articles.title: Catch leaked secrets before `git push`, with one stdlib Python file
articles.excerpt: Everyone has a story about an API key that landed in a public repo. Usually it is not carelessness: a .env file was not in .gitignore yet, or a quick test left a password in a config file, and git add…
articles.body: Everyone has a story about an API key that landed in a public repo. Usually it is not carelessness: a .env file was not in .gitignore yet, or a quick test left a password in a config file, and git add -A did the rest. Dedicated scanners exist, but sometimes you just want a fast local check with no install, no account and no network. So I wrote the env-secrets-scanner skill for Hermes Agent. It ships a single Python script using only the standard library. It walks a folder (or just your staged files), flags real .env files while ignoring .env.example , and matches common token formats: private key blocks, AWS key IDs, GitHub and Slack tokens, JWTs, passwords inside connection URLs, and suspicious password = "..." style assignments. Placeholders like your_key_here are skipped.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.excerpt: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.body: I have been dreaming of doing research in space as an astronaut my whole life, but for some reason, the thought of working underwater made me nervous. I’ve known for a long time that astronauts train underwater to simulate different scenarios they’re likely to experience in space. Diving was never an issue for me, either — I even made it as far as becoming a certified rescue diver. So what was the problem? This summer, I led a simulated space mission in an underwater habitat called the Jules’ Undersea Lab. It is a research station that is located 22 feet (6.7 meters) underwater near Key Largo, Florida. You have to scuba dive to get in and out of the station. To become an aquanaut , you have to stay underwater for at least 24 hours in a so-called state of saturation.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 26, 2004: Cassini spacecraft takes 1st-ever closeup photos of Saturn moon Titan
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 26, 2004, NASA's Cassini spacecraft took the first close-up images of Saturn's largest moon Titan. The Cassini spacecraft would later drop off a probe on Titan named Huygens, which was a European spacecraft that hitched a ride to the Saturn system with the Cassini mission. But before Cassini dropped off its robotic passenger, it flew by Titan a few times and took some amazing photos . Cassini completed its first flyby on July 3, 2004, but when it swung by a second time on Oct. 26, it got about 300 times closer than it did the first time. At the closest point of this flyby, Cassini was 745 miles (1,200 kilometers) away from the surface of Titan. The spacecraft took hundreds of photos during this flyby , and these were the highest resolution views of Titan anyone had ever seen.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering
